title: River landforms: meanders and oxbow lakes

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: How a meander forms and how it can become an oxbow lake.

blocks.heading: How a meander forms
blocks.text: On a bend the water flows fastest on the outside of the curve. It has more energy there, so it erodes the outer bank by hydraulic action and abrasion, and a steep river cliff forms. On the inside of the bend the water is slowest, so it drops some of its load, and a gentle slip-off slope of sand and gravel builds up. Erosion on one side and deposition on the other make the bend larger over time.

blocks.heading: From meander to oxbow lake
blocks.text: As the outer banks of two neighbouring bends are eroded, the neck of land between them becomes narrower. During a flood the river can cut straight through the neck and take the shorter course. Deposition then seals the ends of the old bend, and the water left in it is an oxbow lake.

blocks.heading: Tributary or distributary
blocks.text: A tributary is a smaller river that joins a larger one, so it adds water to it. A distributary does the opposite: it is a channel that splits away from the river and carries some of its water away, as the channels of a delta do near the sea.
